overview: Vulcan Steel is an Australasian-wide industrial products distributor and value-added processor of steel, metals and aluminium, founded in 1995 and dual-listed on the ASX and NZX since its November 2021 IPO. The company operates 81-82 logistics and processing sites employing ~1,650 people across Australia (roughly two-thirds of revenue) and New Zealand (roughly one-third), organized into a Steel segment (distribution, plate/coil processing, rollforming, stainless steel) and a Metals segment (engineering steels and aluminium extrusion/distribution). Growth has been driven by organic greenfield/brownfield site expansion and disciplined M&A, most recently the August 2022 acquisition of Ullrich Aluminium and the September 2025 acquisition of Roofing Industries, a New Zealand roll-formed roofing and cladding manufacturer.

business_model.summary: Vulcan buys steel, aluminium and other metal products from mills and smelters (Asia, Australia, NZ, Europe) and resells them through a distribution network, with a large share of volume value-added through processing (cutting, coil slitting, plate cutting/folding, rollforming, extrusion) before sale to trade and industrial customers. Revenue is transactional/volume-driven (priced per tonne) rather than recurring or contracted, giving it direct exposure to steel/aluminium commodity price cycles, construction activity and industrial production. Growth is pursued via brownfield expansion of existing sites, greenfield entry into new geographies, new product/service categories (stainless, engineering steel, aluminium, rollforming), and bolt-on acquisitions (12 businesses acquired since 1995).

revenue_streams.name: Steel segment (distribution, plate/coil processing, rollforming, stainless)

business_model.customer_type: B2B - trade and industrial customers across manufacturing, engineering, rollformed/sheetmetal, fabricating, transport, mining, and food & agriculture; highly diversified with top customer ~1% of revenue and top 20 customers ~7-13% combined (no material concentration)
business_model.geographic_mix: Australia ~61% (QLD 27%, NSW 19%, VIC 18%, WA 5%, SA 5%, TAS/ACT/NT small), New Zealand ~39% of FY26 group revenue (post-Roofing Industries); historically Australia has run closer to two-thirds of revenue (FY24: AU NZ$698.4m vs NZ NZ$365.9m)

main_competitors: Regional independent steel and metal distributors/fabricators
competitive_position.market_position: One of the largest Australasian-wide industrial metal distributors and value-added processors by site count (81-82 locations) and scale, but operates in a fragmented, competitive market with low switching costs and periodic aggressive discounting by competitors and importers

moat_factors.description: 81-82 strategically located sites across Australia and New Zealand with 'hybridisation' (combining steel and metals/aluminium offerings at one location) creates local service and logistics advantages that are costly for smaller competitors to replicate

Group-wide procurement (e.g., consolidated aluminium purchasing post-Ullrich integration) provides some purchasing power versus smaller independents, though limited pricing power versus large integrated steel makers
Maintains high delivery-in-full-on-time rates (97.9%-98% range) and ~25,000 active customers as a differentiator versus lower-service competitors
Seven industry verticals (steel distribution, plate/coil processing, rollforming, stainless, engineering steel, aluminium) reduce reliance on any single product line and widen customer wallet share
Regional brand strength but steel/metal distribution is largely a commodity, price-competitive business with limited pricing power

weaknesses: Commodity distribution business with thin, cyclical margins and no long-term contracted revenue
Highly fragmented, price-competitive industry; management has flagged 'aggressive, and in our view unsustainable, pricing by some market participants' during FY25 downturn
Limited pricing power - gross margin has compressed from ~35.7% (FY23) to ~33.2% (FY26) amid competitive intensity and mix shift toward lower-margin Metals
High fixed-cost base (leased sites, employees) creates negative operating leverage in downturns - EBITDA fell ~33% in FY24 on a 15% revenue decline
Exposed to import competition from lower-cost fabricated steel, particularly in Australia

growth_drivers: Site hybridisation - converting sites to offer combined steel and metals/aluminium products, improving asset utilisation and cross-sell
Brownfield expansion of existing sites and greenfield entry into new regional markets across Australasia

Roofing Industries acquisition (completed 30 September 2025, ~NZ$88-99m enterprise value) - adds rollforming/roofing vertical, first new product category in years, contributed NZ$155m revenue and ~NZ$25m EBITDA (historical) in its first nine months within Vulcan, expanding to 7 industry verticals across 81 sites and ~25,000 customers
New Zealand cyclical recovery - lower interest rates beginning to stimulate residential and (with a lag) non-residential construction activity; management sees increasing confidence into FY27

Australian infrastructure tailwinds - 2032 Brisbane Olympics construction pipeline (Queensland is ~23-27% of group revenue), though management does not expect meaningful Olympic-related impact until FY27

Potential regulatory tailwind from Australian Productivity Commission inquiry into imported fabricated steel, which could support domestic distributors/processors if safeguard measures are implemented
Further bolt-on M&A - company has integrated 12 acquisitions since 1995 and continues to screen further opportunities
First year-on-year volume growth since FY22 achieved in 1H FY26, suggesting the multi-year industry destocking/downturn cycle may be troughing

business.description: Revenue and EBITDA are highly sensitive to Australian/NZ construction and industrial activity; FY24 saw revenue -14.5% and EBITDA -29.3% YoY, with gross margin per tonne falling ~13% in Steel segment alone

Management explicitly cited 'aggressive, and in our view unsustainable, pricing by some market participants' during FY25, plus one competitor's stock discounting/consolidation noted in 1H FY26; gross margin has trended down from 35.7% (FY23) to 33.2% (FY26)

Roofing Industries (Sept 2025) is Vulcan's largest acquisition since Ullrich Aluminium (2022); integration is described as progressing well but the rollforming vertical is new to the group and carries execution risk, plus a non-controlling interest structure was introduced with the deal
Business is fundamentally transactional/spot-priced distribution with no recurring subscription-like revenue, limiting earnings visibility

financial.risk: Elevated leverage and balance sheet stress
financial.description: Net debt-to-EBITDA (pre-IFRS16) peaked around 3.5x in FY24/early FY25 before improving to 2.9x by FY26 year-end; the bank syndicate first granted a covenant relaxation in October 2024 (after EBITDA fell 30% YoY in the September 2024 quarter) and has since extended that relaxation twice, most recently from 31 December 2025 to 30 June 2026 - signalling the banks still see headroom risk over a year after the original relaxation was granted

financial.risk: Large lease liabilities alongside bank debt
financial.description: IFRS-16 lease liabilities (NZ$290.3m at FY24, NZ$359.7m at 1H FY26) are comparable to or larger than bank net debt (NZ$275.8m FY24, NZ$202-227m FY26), materially increasing total funds-employed leverage beyond what headline 'net bank debt' suggests

A ~NZ$88-96m capital raise to fund the Roofing Industries acquisition lifted shareholders' funds from NZ$169.7m to NZ$288.7m in 1H FY26, diluting existing holders even as it de-risked the balance sheet
FY26 operating cash flow fell ~30% YoY to NZ$73m despite higher EBITDA, reflecting working capital build (inventory, receivables) as volumes recover; 1H FY26 OCF fell 52% YoY
AUD-denominated Australian earnings (majority of group) translated into NZD reporting currency creates FX translation risk

regulatory.description: Outcome of the Australian Productivity Commission inquiry into imported fabricated steel is uncertain - could be a tailwind if safeguard measures favor domestic processors, but the status quo of import competition remains a risk

Steel/metal handling and trucking operations carry inherent workplace safety risk; company has invested in safety systems (Inviol AI platform) but industry has inherent risk of incidents and associated liability

macro.description: Business is a direct proxy for construction and industrial investment activity in Australia and NZ, both of which were suppressed by high interest rates through FY24-FY25; recovery is contingent on continued rate easing flowing through to residential and non-residential building activity
Steel prices have remained subdued while aluminium and nickel prices rose materially in FY26 H2, creating margin timing risk on Vulcan's inventory and pass-through pricing

macro.risk: General election / policy uncertainty in New Zealand
macro.description: Management flagged the NZ general election as a potential dampener on confidence and activity in 2H FY26/into FY27
As a distributor to construction, manufacturing, mining and transport sectors, Vulcan has high operating leverage to any renewed economic slowdown in either Australia or New Zealand

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Australasian steel/metals distribution demand is emerging from a multi-year downturn (FY24-FY25) driven by high interest rates and destocking; early FY26 data shows volume stabilising and modestly recovering in both Australia and New Zealand, with New Zealand's recovery running ahead of Australia's on the back of earlier and larger interest rate cuts
macro_factors.cyclicality: High - revenue and margins are strongly correlated with construction, manufacturing and industrial investment cycles in Australia and New Zealand; demonstrated by ~15% revenue decline and ~29% EBITDA decline in FY24 alone
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: High (indirect) - end-market demand (residential/non-residential construction, industrial investment) is highly sensitive to RBA/RBNZ policy rates; company's own debt is also rate-sensitive (variable-rate bank facilities)
key_input_costs: Labour (largest OPEX line at ~60%+ of total)

recent_developments.event: FY26 full-year results released: revenue NZ$1,159m (+22% YoY, including 9 months of Roofing Industries), adjusted EBITDA NZ$130m (+16% YoY), gross margin 33.2% (down ~1pp), net debt NZ$227m (2.9x post-rent EBITDA, improved from 3.4x), full-year dividend NZ 7.0 cents (+16.7% YoY, 47% payout ratio), FY27 capex guidance NZ$30-35m

1H FY26 results: revenue NZ$535.4m (+8.6% YoY), adjusted EBITDA NZ$57.3m (flat YoY), net debt reduced to NZ$202.3m (2.9x, down from NZ$241.5m a year earlier), first YoY sales volume growth since FY22, interim dividend maintained at NZ 2.5 cents
Completed final settlement payment for Roofing Industries acquisition

CEO transition completed: Gavin Street (Chief Commercial Officer, joined Vulcan 2024) became Managing Director and CEO; long-serving CEO Rhys Jones (19 years) moved to non-executive Chair; former Chair Russell Chenu became lead independent director
Expanded into the New Zealand rollforming market via Roofing Industries integration; opened new rollforming/product category, described as a 'key plank' of growth strategy

Completed acquisition of Roofing Industries Limited, a ~26-year-old New Zealand roll-formed roofing and cladding manufacturer with >NZ$160m revenue and ~NZ$25m EBITDA in its last full year, for ~NZ$88m raised via equity plus an enterprise value of ~NZ$99m; funded partly via a ~NZ$88-96m capital raising

Banking syndicate extended the financial covenant relaxation (originally granted October 2024, initially due to expire 31 December 2025) out to 30 June 2026, while the company confirmed it remained in compliance with covenants; company noted no debt facilities mature before FY2027

FY25 preliminary trading update (full audited FY25 annual report not separately downloaded in this dataset): EBITDA guided to NZ$106-109m, NPAT NZ$14-16m (including ~NZ$3m Wintec asset-sale impairment), net debt reduced to NZ$232m (from NZ$242m at 31 Dec 2024 and NZ$276m at FY24 year-end); management cited 'persistent economic challenges,' 'aggressive, and in our view unsustainable, pricing by some market participants,' but noted early signs of stabilisation and improving momentum

Original covenant relaxation granted by banking syndicate after EBITDA fell ~30% YoY to NZ$33.1m in the September 2024 quarter, with revenue down 13% and volumes down 10%; 1H FY25 profit fell 64.8% YoY to NZ$9.2m

guidance.as_of: FY26 Results (25 August 2026) and FY26 Earnings Call

items.notes: Same range as FY26 guidance; includes continued Roofing Industries investment and carryover growth projects
FY26 actual payout ratio was 47%, within the stated range; FY26 total dividend NZ 7.0 cents, up 16.7% YoY

items.target: Full 12-month earnings contribution vs. 9 months in FY26
items.notes: Roofing Industries generated NZ$155m revenue and an annualised ~NZ$10m NPAT contribution in its first 9 months within the group

items.target: Qualitative - momentum to strengthen through FY27
items.notes: NZ: supportive lower interest rates driving improved activity, commercial recovery likely to lag residential; Australia: high rates remain a cap on growth, but Queensland Olympic-related construction and a possible Productivity Commission safeguard on imported fabricated steel are potential tailwinds, with limited Olympic impact expected until FY27

guidance.management_commentary: New CEO Gavin Street (effective 1 January 2026) and the FY26 results emphasized that industry conditions are stabilising with 'signs of recovery' after the FY24-FY25 downturn, citing the first year-on-year volume growth since FY22 achieved in 1H FY26 and steel volumes up ~20% in H2 FY26. Net debt cover improved to 2.9x (post-rent EBITDA) from a peak of ~3.4-3.5x, aided by the Roofing Industries equity raise and working capital discipline. Management flagged continued cost inflation (underlying OPEX growth ~8-9% YoY ex-Roofing/FX) and gross margin compression from competitive intensity and Metals segment mix as ongoing headwinds, alongside geopolitical and trade-policy uncertainty.

bull_case: Cyclical trough appears to be passing - FY26 delivered the first year-on-year volume growth since FY22, with steel volumes up ~20% in H2 FY26 and both Australian and New Zealand end markets showing early recovery signs as interest rates ease

Roofing Industries acquisition diversifies the business into a new, historically higher-margin rollforming/roofing vertical, adding ~NZ$155m of revenue and ~NZ$25m of historical EBITDA, with integration reported as going well and a full 12-month contribution to flow through in FY27

Balance sheet has materially de-risked - net debt roughly halved from the FY23 peak (NZ$339.7m) to NZ$202-227m by FY26, leverage improved from ~3.5x to 2.9x, and the dilutive equity raise reduces near-term refinancing/covenant risk even as it holds the banks' relaxation window open through June 2026

Diversified, granular customer base (~25,000 active customers, no material customer concentration) and broad geographic/product footprint (81+ sites, 7 verticals) reduce single-point-of-failure risk and provide multiple growth levers (hybridisation, greenfield, bolt-on M&A)

Potential structural tailwinds from Australian infrastructure/Olympics-related construction demand in Queensland and a possible regulatory safeguard on imported fabricated steel, alongside a New Zealand economic recovery that historically leads the cycle
bear_case: Two-year covenant relaxation history (Oct 2024 to now June 2026, extended twice) signals the banking syndicate still sees meaningful headroom risk more than 18 months after the original earnings shock - this is not a business operating from a position of clear financial strength

Structurally thin, commoditised distribution margins with limited pricing power - gross margin has compressed from 35.7% (FY23) to 33.2% (FY26) amid what management itself calls 'aggressive, and in our view unsustainable, pricing' from competitors, with no clear catalyst to reverse the trend

High operating leverage to a cyclical, rate-sensitive end market already demonstrated in FY24 (EBITDA -29% on a 15% revenue decline) and FY25 (NPAT guided to just NZ$14-16m, down from NZ$95m adjusted in FY23) - any stalling of the rate-cutting cycle in Australia or New Zealand would quickly pressure earnings again

Total leverage understates true obligations if lease liabilities are included - IFRS-16 lease liabilities (NZ$359.7m at 1H FY26) now exceed bank net debt, and funds employed of ~NZ$491m dwarfs shareholders' funds even after the FY26 equity raise

Integration and execution risk from the Roofing Industries acquisition and a newly installed CEO (effective January 2026, in the role less than a year) create leadership and M&A-digestion uncertainty at a delicate point in the earnings recovery

Recent equity raise (~NZ$88-96m) diluted existing shareholders and operating cash flow fell ~30% YoY in FY26 despite higher EBITDA, driven by working capital rebuild - a reminder that reported earnings growth is not yet translating cleanly into free cash flow
